rationale: B wins by a slight margin because its journalist shape is sharper and its proof demands are more newsroom-real: “a merchant-acquiring or retail-operations trade outlet” plus “Without merchant reaction this is a vendor announcement with a hostile headline on it” tells the founder exactly where the story lives and what will kill it. A is cleaner and very usable, especially “Flat fee vs. interchange: the math behind Plaid's ‘up to 70% cheaper’ claim,” but it is safer and less precise about the reporting paths. B's invented category context keeps this from being a clean win.
gaps_in_A: “A payments-industry reporter at a fintech or banking trade outlet” is looser than it should be; payments trades, merchant-acquiring trades, and banking-tech outlets are not the same desk.

“FedNow gets a merchant-facing on-ramp through Plaid's 12,000 bank connections” risks implying those 12,000 institutions are FedNow-ready; A asks for proof later, but the headline still leans on the stronger version.
“The card networks are the story” and “the fee math” overlap a bit; the merchant-cost and incumbent-network angles are related enough that A needed cleaner separation.
A misses the obvious bank-side and consumer-protection questions: who loses card revenue, and who handles disputes or fraud when a card rail is bypassed.
gaps_in_B: “FedNow adoption stories have mostly been about disbursements and B2B” is unsourced context not supplied in the update.
“The prevailing belief in the category is that pay-by-bank is a general-purpose card replacement” is invented; no supplied fact establishes that belief.
“The 70% saving only shows up on big-ticket sales” overstates the update; Plaid only says early merchants see fees up to 70% lower on large transactions.
“Plaid needs 12,000 banks to help route payments past the fees banks collect” is a sharp angle with unproven bank-revenue mechanics; B admits the inference, but the headline still carries it as fact.
